chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ali ibn Bilal, from Al-Hasan ibn Bassam Al-Jammal, from a man who said:

I was with Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) in what is between Makkah and Al-Medina in the month of Sha'ban, and he was fasting. Then we saw the crescent of the month of Ramadan, so he broke his fast. So I said to him, 'May I be sacrificed for you! Yesterday was from Sha'ban and you were fasting, and today is from the month of Ramadan and you are not fasting?' So he said: 'That was voluntary (fasting), and for us is that we do what we so desire to, and this is an Obligation, so it is not for us that we do except for what we have been Commanded for'.

key_terms.أَفْطَرَ: Broke the fast (ended the daily fast)
key_terms.تَطَوُّعٌ: Voluntary (referring to non-obligatory acts of worship)
key_terms.رَمَضَانَ: Ramadan (the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar, month of fasting)
key_terms.شَعْبَانَ: Sha'ban (the eighth month of the Islamic lunar calendar)
key_terms.صَائِمٌ: Fasting (abstaining from food, drink, etc. from dawn to sunset)
key_terms.فَرْضٌ: Obligation (referring to mandatory acts of worship)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between voluntary and obligatory fasting according to the Imams?
ai.summary: Although the chain attributes the narration to Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib (AS), it is frequently cited in Shia jurisprudence (fiqh) to illustrate the flexibility of voluntary (nafl) fasting during travel, contrasting it with the strict obligation of Ramadan. The Imam’s distinction highlights that while obligatory duties are fixed by divine command, voluntary acts remain under the individual's discretion, a principle crucial for understanding the rulings on qada (making up) and nafl fasts in Shia legal theory.
